view.mode.title: Plain or Technical
view.mode.what: Plain shows short explanations in everyday words. Technical adds the API calls, the checks behind each decision and the tools used.
view.mode.why: Owners, firms and developers can read the same page at the level that suits them.

view.labels.title: Info labels
view.labels.what: Shows or hides the word "info" beside each i button.
view.labels.why: The i buttons always work. The label makes them easier to spot on a first visit.

view.theme.title: Theme
view.theme.what: Light is the default. Dark is easier on the eyes at night. System follows your device setting.
view.theme.why: Choose whichever is most comfortable to read.

view.text.title: Text size
view.text.what: Large makes all text about a fifth bigger.
view.text.why: Comfortable reading for everyone, including people with low vision.

page.home.title: About this page
page.home.what: Remedy pays recall refunds the moment a photo is verified. Try a photo, or take the 2-minute tour.
page.home.why: Many recalls already ask owners to send a photo of the product made safe. Remedy turns that photo into a refund in seconds.
page.home.technical: Each recall's remedy becomes a structured proof rule. A photo is checked against it, and a verified claim is paid through PayPal Payouts or refunded to the original PayPal purchase.

how.steps.title: How it works
how.steps.what: The recall is read into a checklist, you snap a photo, the photo is checked, and PayPal pays you.
how.steps.why: Each step is one the recall already asks for. Remedy makes the wait between them seconds instead of weeks.
how.steps.technical: Proof rule (Claude Opus 5.5, structured output), then checks C1 to C6, then a decision made in code, then a PayPal payout or a refund to the original capture.

page.try.title: About this page
page.try.what: Try Remedy with one of our sample photos or your own, and see each check and the result.
page.try.why: It is the quickest way to see a photo become a refund.
page.try.technical: Payouts here come from the sample firm's PayPal sandbox account. Demonstration in PayPal sandbox. Remedy is not affiliated with the recalling firm.

page.recalls.title: About this page
page.recalls.what: Every US consumer product recall since January 2024 from the CPSC, with the ones that offer a refund for a photo marked.
page.recalls.why: Find your recall, read what it asks you to do, and start a claim.
page.recalls.technical: Recall data comes from the CPSC Recalls API, which is public. Search is hybrid keyword and semantic search on Elastic.

page.evidence.title: About this page
page.evidence.what: Every number on this site, where it comes from, and a five-minute path through the product.
page.evidence.why: So you can see the whole loop, from a recall to a paid refund, without hunting for it.
page.evidence.technical: Every payout and refund runs in the PayPal sandbox. The test commands and their results are listed in the project's TESTING.md.

page.learn.title: About this page
page.learn.what: How product recalls work, the words used on this site, and where our numbers come from.
page.learn.why: Plain answers make it easier to act on a recall.
page.learn.technical: Figures come from the CPSC Recalls API (public domain). Each one names its date range and how it was counted.

page.about.title: About this page
page.about.what: What Remedy is, and how it labels what is real and what is a sample.
page.about.why: So you know what you are looking at.
page.about.technical: Remedy is open source under the MIT license. The sample firm, Brightline Home, is fictional.

page.firm.title: About this page
page.firm.what: The console for a recalling firm: the claims to review, the recall plan and the monthly report.
page.firm.why: Small firms handle recall claims by hand today. This puts every claim, payment and deadline in one place.
page.firm.technical: Brightline Home is a fictional sample firm. Its payouts run from a PayPal sandbox account.

page.developers.title: About this page
page.developers.what: Everything a developer needs to add verify-and-refund to a recall page: a free key, a live playground and code samples.
page.developers.why: Marketplaces, recall service providers and AI agents can verify a photo and pay a refund with one call.
page.developers.technical: Keys are rm_test_ plus 32 random bytes in base62. Only the SHA-256 hash is stored. Limits are counted per key in Postgres.

page.keys.title: About this page
page.keys.what: The keys created in this browser, the calls they made, and buttons to rotate or revoke them.
page.keys.why: You stay in control of every key.
page.keys.technical: GET /api/keys reads usage from the api_usage table. Rotate issues a new key and revokes the old one in one step.

page.docs.title: About this page
page.docs.what: The reference for every endpoint: fields, examples, errors and limits.
page.docs.why: So you can build against the API without guessing.
page.docs.technical: Field tables are generated from the Zod schemas every request is validated with, the same source as /openapi.json.

page.status.title: About this page
page.status.what: A check of every service Remedy uses: PayPal, Claude, the database and each tool it is built on.
page.status.why: If a service is not connected, Remedy uses its fallback so every flow keeps working. This page shows which mode each one is in. An optional add-on that is not switched on, such as Sentry error tracking, reads Optional, off and is not counted against the live total.
page.status.technical: GET /api/health runs the same checks and returns JSON, with a summary that leaves optional add-ons that are off out of the total. PayPal and Postgres answer a real call; the rest are read from their settings.

dev.keys.title: Sandbox keys
dev.keys.what: A free key for testing. It is shown once; Remedy keeps only a fingerprint of it.
dev.keys.why: Keys give you higher limits and a usage page, and you can rotate or revoke them anytime.
dev.keys.technical: POST /api/keys returns the key once. Rotate and revoke are tied to this browser through an httpOnly cookie, with no passwords.

dev.playground.title: Playground
dev.playground.what: Send real requests to the live API and see the full response, plus the same call in cURL, JavaScript and Python.
dev.playground.why: You can see exactly what your code will get back before you write it.
dev.playground.technical: Requests go to the same endpoints your code will call, through the same key check and rate limits.

stack.strip.title: Every tool, with a job
stack.strip.what: These are the tools Remedy is built with. Each one does one specific job here.
stack.strip.why: Open any name to see what it does in Remedy, or visit How it is built for where each one lives in the code.

stack.paypal.title: PayPal
stack.paypal.what: Pays refunds instantly, and refunds to the original purchase inside 180 days.
stack.paypal.why: An owner who made the product safe gets the money in seconds, the way they already get paid by friends.
stack.paypal.technical: Payouts (email, phone, Venmo), Payments v2 refunds to the original capture, Orders v2 and the JavaScript SDK v6, with webhooks verified with PayPal by signature or by looking the event up. Sandbox only.

stack.claude.title: Claude Opus 5.5
stack.claude.what: Reads each recall's remedy into a checklist, checks photos, and runs the two reviewers.
stack.claude.why: Recall remedies are written as free text. A clear checklist tells the owner exactly what to do and what the photo must show.
stack.claude.technical: claude-opus-5-5 with structured outputs validated by Zod. Rules for every photo-refund recall are extracted with the Message Batches API. The decision and the money are plain code.

stack.elastic.title: Elastic
stack.elastic.what: Searches every recall in plain words: keyword and semantic, reranked.
stack.elastic.why: Owners describe products in their own words. Search that understands meaning finds the right recall.
stack.elastic.technical: Hybrid search: keyword and semantic retrieval fused by reciprocal rank, then reranked. An in-app keyword search stands in when Elastic is not connected.

stack.channel3.title: Channel3
stack.channel3.what: Finds a safe replacement product for an owner who would rather have one.
stack.channel3.why: Some owners need the product, not the money. Each replacement is checked against active recalls first.
stack.channel3.technical: POST /v1/search for in-stock products in the same category and price range, then GET /v1/products/{id} for the current offer.

stack.bryntum.title: Bryntum
stack.bryntum.what: The firm's corrective-action plan and review schedule, as a timeline.
stack.bryntum.why: A recall has deadlines: notices, payouts, follow-ups and monthly reports. The plan keeps them in order and updates itself.
stack.bryntum.technical: Bryntum Gantt 7.3 (trial), loaded as a script and themed to match the site. Payout webhooks add follow-up tasks to the plan.

stack.ag-grid.title: AG Grid
stack.ag-grid.why: A reviewer sees every claim with its photo and checks in one place, and pays verified claims in bulk.
stack.ag-grid.technical: AG Grid 36 for the claims queue: Community modules always, and with a valid Enterprise license key, set filters, the column menu and the status bar too.

stack.render.title: Render
stack.render.what: Hosts the site and its Postgres database.
stack.render.why: One place runs the site and keeps every record.
stack.render.technical: render.yaml defines the web service and managed Postgres. Tables come from the reviewed SQL in db/schema.sql.

stack.postgres.title: Postgres
stack.postgres.what: Keeps every recall, claim, payment and plan task, and the audit ledger.
stack.postgres.why: Every refund can be traced back to its claim, its photo and its checks.
stack.postgres.technical: Postgres 17 with the tables in db/schema.sql. The audit ledger is hash-chained, so any changed entry shows.

stack.paypal_apis.title: Every PayPal API Remedy calls
stack.paypal_apis.what: Each PayPal API Remedy uses, the call it makes, and the one job it does here.
stack.paypal_apis.why: PayPal is how the refund reaches the owner: every payout, refund and order goes through these calls.
stack.paypal_apis.technical: Every call, from Payouts and refunds to Orders, Transaction Search, Disputes and webhook checks, uses fetch with one cached OAuth token.

intro.stat.title: How this was counted
intro.stat.what: Out of every US consumer product recall the CPSC published since January 2024, these are the ones whose remedy asks for a photo of the product made safe and pays a refund for it.
intro.stat.why: Many recalls already pay on a photo. Remedy makes that photo quick to check and quick to pay.
intro.stat.technical: CPSC Recalls API, every recall dated on or after 2024-01-01. First the remedy text must name a photo and a refund (/photo|picture|image/i and /refund/i, src/lib/recall/classify.ts). Then the recall's proof rule must list a made-safe action (cut, mark, remove a part) and a refund in money, not store credit (src/lib/recall/made-safe.ts). The counts, with every recall left out and why, are in content/recalls/proof-split.json.

showcase.search.title: Recall search
showcase.search.what: Type what you bought. The three closest recalls appear, each with what it asks you to do and what you get.
showcase.search.why: People describe products in their own words, not by recall number.
showcase.search.technical: GET /api/v1/recalls?query=: Elastic keyword and semantic search fused by reciprocal rank, reranked, with an in-app keyword ranking as the fallback. The chips come from each recall's stored proof rule.

try.panel.title: The photo checks
try.panel.what: Each sample photo goes through the same checks a real claim does: right product, made safe, your own photo, within the recall, claim limits, and not already refunded.
try.panel.why: A refund should go to someone who has the recalled product and made it safe. The checks keep the refund pool for real owners.
try.panel.technical: Runs of verifyPhoto: the recorded ones in content/public/verify-runs.json, and the CPSC's 26125 photo run through the claim path when the page is built, where the free picture match answers it. The free checks (quality, and the match against the recall's official images and earlier claims) need no AI. The vision checks use Claude Opus 5.5 with structured output; the decision, the amount and the payment route are plain code.

stats.figures.title: These figures
stats.figures.what: Every figure is counted from the CPSC's public recall data, for the dates shown.
stats.figures.why: So you can check each one yourself.
stats.figures.technical: content/recalls/stats.json, written by scripts/recalls/stats.ts from the CPSC Recalls API. Units use the first number in the first product's NumberOfUnits, as the CPSC states it for the US.

research.row.title: The sources
research.row.what: The public data and research Remedy is built on, with what each one says.
research.row.why: A faster, fuller remedy is the direction the research and the regulator point to.
research.row.technical: Each link goes to the source itself: the CPSC's own pages and the published study.

dev.fragment.title: This example
dev.fragment.what: A real request to Remedy's API and the answer it gives today for recall 27056, a power bank recall.
dev.fragment.why: Any recall page can show the owner the same checklist.
dev.fragment.technical: Rendered from the stored rule in content/recalls/proof-rules.json, the same data POST /api/v1/proof-rule returns.

recalls.filters.title: Filters
recalls.filters.what: Narrow the list to recalls that refund a photo, a year, a kind of product, a remedy, or how many units were recalled.
recalls.filters.why: So you can find your recall, or study a group of them.
recalls.filters.technical: The same filters as GET /api/v1/recalls. With search words, Elastic ranks the closest 30; the remedy and units filters then apply to those.

recall.rule.title: The proof rule
recall.rule.what: The recall's remedy read as a checklist: what to do to the product, what the photo must show, and what you get.
recall.rule.why: The official remedy is written for lawyers. The checklist is written for you, and Remedy checks photos against it.
recall.rule.technical: Claude Opus 5.5 with structured output at medium effort, then a self-check pass against the remedy text and a deterministic lint, run for every photo-refund recall with the Message Batches API. Confidence is the model's own, per field.

recall.images.title: Official images
recall.images.what: The pictures the CPSC published with this recall.
recall.images.why: They help you check that you have the recalled product. Remedy also uses them to make sure each claim photo is the owner's own.
recall.images.technical: Each image's perceptual hash (64-bit dHash) is stored; a claim photo within 10 bits of one is asked to be the owner's own photo.

recall.images.sample.title: The recall's photos
recall.images.sample.what: Photos of the sample product, published with Brightline Home's fictional sample recall.
recall.images.sample.why: They help you check that you have the recalled charger. Remedy also uses them to make sure each claim photo is the owner's own.
recall.images.sample.technical: Public-domain photos of one real laptop charger by Dmitry G on Wikimedia Commons, brand marks removed (public/samples/charger/CREDITS.json). Each one's perceptual hash (64-bit dHash) is stored, as for a CPSC recall's official images.

recall.remedy.title: The official remedy
recall.remedy.what: The remedy exactly as the CPSC published it, word for word.
recall.remedy.why: The checklist above is read from these words, so you can compare them.
recall.remedy.technical: Remedies[].Name from the CPSC Recalls API, joined in order.

recall.technical.title: Behind this rule
recall.technical.what: The raw CPSC record and how the rule was made: Claude's first draft, the self-check, and what the self-check changed.
recall.technical.why: So a reviewer can trace every field of the rule back to the source.
recall.technical.technical: Drafts and checks come from content/recalls/extract (Message Batches, with their batch ids and token counts). The raw record is from the CPSC Recalls API pull.

evidence.results.title: The results
evidence.results.what: The four numbers to know, each with where it comes from. Open any section below for the full detail.
evidence.results.why: Five minutes is enough to see the loop and to check the data behind it.
evidence.results.technical: Read from content/recalls/stats.json, content/recalls/benchmark/results.json and content/public/verify-runs.json.

evidence.benchmark.title: The extraction benchmark
evidence.benchmark.what: 130 real CPSC remedies, read by three systems, scored field by field against labels.
evidence.benchmark.why: Every check depends on reading the remedy right, so we measured it on public data we did not write.
evidence.benchmark.technical: A stratified random sample of 100 photo-refund remedies and 30 others. Systems: a regular-expression reader, Claude Opus 5.5, and Claude with a self-check. Exact match per field; actions and must_show also as precision and recall. The labels are a draft and are being checked by hand.

evidence.fixtures.title: The photo checks, recorded
evidence.fixtures.what: Each photo case the verifier was run on, and what it decided.
evidence.fixtures.why: The checks keep the refund pool for real owners: the recall's own pictures, copies of them, and photos already used are each caught.
evidence.fixtures.technical: verifyPhoto on content/verify/fixtures. Cases with no vision need no AI; two vision cases are recorded live runs of Claude Opus 5.5. Written by scripts/public/record-runs.ts.

evidence.compare.title: How it compares
evidence.compare.what: How a photo-refund claim works today by email, through a recall vendor's portal, and on Remedy.
evidence.compare.why: Each of these does its job well. Remedy adds the instant check and the PayPal payout to what firms already do.

evidence.adoption.title: Who runs it first
evidence.adoption.what: The groups that could use Remedy as it is today, with the numbers behind each.
evidence.adoption.why: Most recalls are small, and small firms handle claims by hand.

learn.rule.title: What a proof rule is
learn.rule.what: A recall's remedy written as fields a person and a program can both read: what to do, what the photo shows, what you get.
learn.rule.why: One clear rule means the owner, the firm and the checker all expect the same photo.
learn.rule.technical: Schema in src/lib/recall/proof-rule.ts: photo_required, actions, marker_text, must_show, remedy, refund_amount, contact_channel, steps, explanation and confidence.

status.ai_spend.title: AI spend today
status.ai_spend.what: What Remedy's Claude calls have cost so far today, from its own log of every live call, broken down by what each call was for.
status.ai_spend.why: The hosted site keeps to a daily cap. Past it, photos still get every free check, and a person at the firm looks at the rest.
status.ai_spend.technical: Each live call is logged to the ai_usage table with its input, output and cache token counts; cost is those counts times the published per-model rates (src/lib/ai/usage.ts). Repeated identical requests replay and cost nothing.

dev.mcp.title: MCP server
dev.mcp.what: AI assistants can search recalls, read a proof rule, check a photo and open a claim with Remedy's tools.
dev.mcp.why: An assistant helping someone with a recall can give exact steps, and the owner still chooses where the refund goes.
dev.mcp.technical: Model Context Protocol over streamable HTTP at /api/mcp, stateless JSON-RPC. Seven tools: search_recalls, scan_catalog, get_proof_rule, verify_photo, open_claim, claim_status and ping. Discovery: /api/mcp/server-card and /.well-known/ai-catalog.json.

dev.mcp-session.title: The recorded session
dev.mcp-session.what: The tool calls an AI assistant makes to help an owner: find the recall, read what it asks, give the owner their claim link, open the claim with their photo, and follow it.
dev.mcp-session.why: It shows the whole path an assistant can take for an owner, with the owner still choosing where the refund goes.
dev.mcp-session.technical: Real JSON-RPC tools/call requests to /api/mcp, recorded by scripts/public/record-mcp-session.mjs into content/public/mcp-session.json. No AI model was called to record them: the photo is Brightline's published sample photo, answered by the verification cache. The claim it opened was removed afterwards.

stack.apimatic.title: APIMatic
stack.apimatic.what: Generated the PayPal Server SDK that Remedy uses for every order, capture and refund.
stack.apimatic.why: A typed SDK catches mistakes in PayPal requests before they reach PayPal.
stack.apimatic.technical: @paypal/paypal-server-sdk (APIMatic): OrdersController for create, get and capture; PaymentsController for captures and refunds, each with PayPal-Request-Id. Payouts, Transaction Search and Disputes use REST, which the SDK does not cover.

stack.recall-ingest.title: Daily recall ingest
stack.recall-ingest.what: Once a day Remedy pulls every new CPSC recall, reads its remedy into a proof rule, hashes its official images and adds it to search.
stack.recall-ingest.why: New photo-refund recalls appear in 2026 at about one a day, so owners of the newest ones can claim without waiting for a release.
stack.recall-ingest.technical: A Render cron job calls POST /api/ops/recalls/daily with CHECKS_SECRET. New rows go to recall, proof_rule and image_hash in Postgres and to the Elastic index; the committed JSON files are never written. Claude Opus 5.5 reads each new photo-refund rule with a self-check, inside the daily AI budget.

dev.embed.title: The recall badge
dev.embed.what: A small page our server renders for an iframe: the recall, its one-line remedy and refund, and a link to the owner's claim page.
dev.embed.why: A product page or a listing can show the remedy where the owner is, with nothing to build and nothing else loaded on the page.
dev.embed.technical: GET /api/embed/badge?recall= or ?q= (the best-matching recall). Inputs are escaped; the page sets frame-ancestors * and a strict CSP of its own, and follows prefers-color-scheme. /api/embed/badge.js inserts the iframe where the script tag sits.

stack.queue.title: Job queue
stack.queue.what: Photo checks and payouts run as jobs in a queue, not inside the web request. This row shows how many are waiting, the oldest one, and any that stopped after five tries.
stack.queue.why: A slow check or a PayPal pause never blocks the page or the next owner; the job is tried again on its own, and a person sees the few that still need help.
stack.queue.technical: The job table (db/schema.sql). A worker takes the next row with select ... for update skip locked, retries with exponential backoff (1, 2, 4, 8 s) up to 5 attempts, and leaves a failed row with its error as the dead letter. src/lib/jobs.

stack.worker.title: Worker
stack.worker.what: The separate process that runs the jobs. It reports in every 30 seconds; this row says when it was last seen.
stack.worker.why: Checks and payouts keep running when the web service is busy or restarting, and the site keeps answering while a check runs.
stack.worker.technical: scripts/worker.ts, a Render background worker (render.yaml) or npm run worker locally. Heartbeat: an integration_status row updated every 30 s. Without a worker for 2 s, the route runs its own job inline and logs that it did.

stack.error-tracking.title: Error tracking
stack.error-tracking.what: Unexpected errors on the server and in the browser are sent to Sentry, with every personal detail removed first, so they can be fixed before anyone reports them.
stack.error-tracking.why: A problem an owner hits once at night is seen the same hour, with the request id to trace it.
stack.error-tracking.technical: @sentry/nextjs, on only when SENTRY_DSN is set. sendDefaultPii is off and beforeSend masks emails, phone numbers, photo data and keys (src/lib/sentry.ts). Release is the git commit; environment is the Render service.

page.ops.title: About this page
page.ops.what: Everything Remedy watches about itself, live: each service, the job queue, request latency and errors, payments and webhooks by status, and the event stream. Read only, and nothing on it is private.
page.ops.why: Anyone can see the site is healthy, and anyone can paste a request id and follow it from the API answer to the ledger.
page.ops.technical: Every figure comes from tables the app already writes: request_log, audit_event, api_usage, ai_usage, payment, webhook_event, job and integration_status (src/lib/ops/data.ts). The stream is Server-Sent Events from GET /api/ops/live.

ops.now.title: Right now
ops.now.what: Each service live or on its fallback, how many jobs are waiting, what today's AI calls have cost against the cap, and requests in the last hour.
ops.now.why: The first thing an operator looks at: is everything up, and is anything piling up.
ops.now.technical: runChecks (src/lib/health.ts), queueStats (src/lib/jobs/queue.ts), spendToday (ai_usage) and a count over request_log for the last hour.

ops.day.title: Last 24 hours
ops.day.what: Requests by route with their typical and slow latency and error rate; payments, webhooks and photo decisions by status; AI calls and cost by route.
ops.day.why: Counts only, so the day's shape is public while every owner and payee stays private.
ops.day.technical: request_log grouped by route with percentile_cont(0.5) and (0.95) over ms; payment and payment_plan by status; webhook_event by verified; claim by decision; ai_usage by route.

ops.stream.title: Live stream
ops.stream.what: The newest ledger entries and API requests as one feed, newest first, updating every two seconds.
ops.stream.why: Shows the site working in real time. Ids are shortened and nothing names a person.
ops.stream.technical: GET /api/ops/live streams Server-Sent Events (the same pattern as the firm console). With reduced motion on, the page shows a Refresh button instead and reads ?once=1.

ops.chart.title: Reliability over time
ops.chart.what: Requests and errors per hour over the last seven days.
ops.chart.why: A week at a glance: quiet hours, busy hours, and whether errors track load.
ops.chart.technical: request_log grouped by date_trunc(hour) for 168 hours, drawn as inline SVG in code with the theme's colors; no chart library.

ops.trace.title: Trace a request
ops.trace.what: Paste the request id from any API answer and see that request's log lines and the ledger entries it wrote.
ops.trace.why: Every API error ends with its request id, so anyone can follow one call end to end.
ops.trace.technical: GET /api/ops/trace?id= reads request_log by request_id and audit_event where detail->>'request_id' matches. The id is set in src/lib/log.ts (x-request-id is honored when a caller sends one).

ops.alerts.title: Alerts
ops.alerts.what: The conditions Remedy watches, each computed live: fine when so, attention when not.
ops.alerts.why: No pager is connected to the demo; these are the same checks a pager would get, so the state is visible to anyone.
ops.alerts.technical: src/lib/ops/data.ts alerts(): 5xx rate over 15 minutes, queue age, worker heartbeat, AI spend against AI_DAILY_USD, unverified webhooks, failed payouts, dead-letter jobs.

evidence.load.title: Under load
evidence.load.what: One hundred visitors at once, each running the free paths: a claim with the official picture, a recall search and the catalog scan sample, against the production build on a laptop.
evidence.load.why: Shows what the demo handles as built, measured, not guessed.
evidence.load.technical: scripts/load-test.mjs: 100 concurrent virtual users, p50, p95 and p99 per path and the error rate, written to content/public/load-test.json with the machine and method. The official-picture claim is settled by the perceptual hash, so no model call is made.

evidence.real.title: Running it for real
evidence.real.what: What the demo runs on today, and what a production deployment changes.
evidence.real.why: Stated as an operating range, so a firm knows what to plan for.
evidence.real.technical: render.yaml: one Starter web service, one worker, a 256 MB Postgres. A production copy adds object storage with signed URLs for photos, a larger Postgres with a pooler, autoscaling with the worker, login and roles for firms, a registered webhook per environment, and tested backups. Photo retention is already in code: src/lib/ops/photos.ts deletes a photo that shows a person at once and every owner's photo 90 days after the decision, keeping its hash.

evidence.errors.title: The error rates
evidence.errors.what: The two mistakes that cost money: paying for a photo that should not be paid, and holding back one that could have been paid. Each is counted on every recorded decision where the right answer is known.
evidence.errors.why: A refund engine is only as good as its mistakes. Counting both, with the photos behind them, shows where it pays and where it hands over to a person.
evidence.errors.technical: src/components/evidence/errors.ts reads content/verify/sweep-results.json (the claim path's setting only), content/presets/recorded/*.json and content/public/verify-runs.json when the page is built, and the known answers from content/verify/fixtures/cases.json and content/presets/index.json. A known answer of verified, or right product and made safe both required, counts as paid; any other named decision counts as not paid.

evidence.never.title: What the AI never decides
evidence.never.what: Claude reads the remedy and describes the photo. Whether to pay, how much, to whom and when are plain code.
evidence.never.why: The money path stays predictable and testable, and the model's part can be measured on its own.
evidence.never.technical: The decision is decide() in src/lib/verify/decide.ts; pass marks are LIMITS in src/lib/verify/checks.ts; the amount is computeAmount() there; the route and approval are planPayment() in src/lib/payments/router.ts. Switch Plain or Technical (top right) to Technical to see the file for each line.

evidence.pilot.title: The pilot
evidence.pilot.what: One firm, one recall, 30 days, measured against the month before: the claim rate first (completed claims as a share of the recall's units), then the time from photo to refund, and the share of claims a person had to open.
evidence.pilot.why: The claim rate is what the CPSC measures a recall by; the others are what a firm feels: owners paid sooner, and fewer photos read by hand.
evidence.pilot.technical: Both are already recorded: claim.submitted, claim.decided and claim.paid in the hash-chained audit ledger (GET /api/ledger/verify checks it), the payment's paid_at, and each claim's decision in the claim table, with the firm console's queue views over them.

evidence.research.title: Grounded in research
evidence.research.what: Published findings on recall response, claiming and photo matching, each with what Remedy does about it.
evidence.research.why: A full refund and simple steps are what help owners finish a recall; Remedy is built around both.
evidence.research.technical: Sources: Raithel, Hock and Mafael (2024), Journal of the Academy of Marketing Science 52:716-735; Bhargava and Manoli (2015), American Economic Review 105(11):3489-3529; CPSC news release, January 17, 2025; Krawetz (2013), dHash; PayPal Holdings 3Q 2026 earnings release. The list is src/components/evidence/Research.tsx.

evidence.money.title: What is at stake
evidence.money.what: What the recalls that refund a photo of the product made safe offer their owners, counted from the CPSC records and the proof rules.
evidence.money.why: Every point of return that simpler claiming adds sends real money back to owners, and every product made safe is one fewer hazard in a home.
evidence.money.technical: scripts/recalls/value.ts writes content/recalls/value.json: for each recall whose proof rule asks for a made-safe photo and pays a refund in money, its US units times the lowest price its Sold At field states, or the fixed refund its rule states when that is lower, only where the record states units and a price. Pro-rated refunds state no share and are left out (src/lib/recall/value.ts, tested in tests/recall-value.test.ts). The 6 in 100 is the CPSC measure in src/lib/research.ts.

evidence.first.title: What is first here
evidence.first.what: Three things Remedy does that the nearest existing products and filings, read from their own pages, stop short of: the checked photo paid in the same flow, a hash pool shared across firms, and the refund routed back to the original purchase with an unclaimed payout turned into a task.
evidence.first.why: A claim of novelty is only as good as the comparison beside it, so each line links to the row that shows what exists.
evidence.first.technical: The comparison rows live in src/components/evidence/Compare.tsx (LANDSCAPE), each with its source URL and date; the three statements are in src/app/evidence/page.tsx (FIRST) and point at those rows by id.

evidence.problem.title: The problem, measured
evidence.problem.what: The regulator's own correction rate, its 2026 request for information on recall claims that are not genuine and two comments on that docket, how firms pay photo-proof refunds today, the payment issuers' own terms and costs, and surveys of why owners do not act.
evidence.problem.why: Every figure here is a primary source read on November 8, 2026 and paraphrased, with what Remedy does about it beside it. In Technical view each card also names the code that answers it.
evidence.problem.technical: The figures live in src/lib/research.ts (PROBLEM) with their URLs and page dates; the cards are src/components/evidence/Research.tsx (ProblemResearch). The CPSC listing count is written by scripts/recalls/listing-mentions.ts to content/recalls/listing-mentions.json. The FY2025 correction rate is an average across recalls under a method revised in FY2024, so it is not comparable with the 6 in 100 figure, which is the share of recalled units that come back.

evidence.landscape.title: What exists near Remedy
evidence.landscape.what: Seven products, portals and one patent application that do part of what Remedy does, each described from its own page or filing, with the one step it leaves to others.
evidence.landscape.why: Each does its job. Naming them is how the difference is shown rather than claimed.
evidence.landscape.technical: src/components/evidence/Compare.tsx (LANDSCAPE): Truepic Vision and the Truepic Risk Network, Sedgwick's recall pages, Real Time Results portals, a recall administrator's live photo capture (CPSC docket comment), CCC Estimate-STP and Snapsheet in insurance, and US 2016/0350756 A1 (abandoned 2018). Pages read November 8, 2026.

evidence.lineage.title: The two-reviewer design
evidence.lineage.what: The published work the design rests on, and the part that is new: two reviewers reading two different rulebooks, with a disagreement sent to a person, in payments.
evidence.lineage.why: A model panel built from different model names shares errors; independence has to come from different inputs, so one reviewer sees only the official pictures and the other only the remedy text.
evidence.lineage.technical: src/lib/verify/reviewers.ts runs the two reviewers and the referee, which counts only votes whose cited evidence checks out; src/lib/verify/decide.ts turns the referee's result into verified, retake or a person's review. Papers: Zheng 2023 (arXiv 2306.05685), Madras 2018 (1711.06664), Jung 2024 (2407.18370), Badshah 2026 (2608.17994), Kohli 2026 (2605.29800).
